summary: This Best Current Practice describes how the IETF handles incoming liaison statements from other standards bodies and how it creates its own to send out. The procedure aims to make collaboration with other organisations work smoothly and keep a record.

plainLanguage.summary: When another group sends the IETF an official letter, someone must know where it goes and who answers. This document sets out that mail-handling routine.

questions: how does the ietf handle liaison statements
do ietf have to respond to liaison statements
subtitle: How the IETF receives, tracks, answers and sends official letters to other standards bodies.

tldr.problem: Other standards bodies send the IETF official letters with requests and deadlines, and the IETF has not always handled them well, which frustrated people in those organizations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines what a liaison statement contains, who is responsible for it, how it is submitted and tracked through a web form and email, and how the IETF answers or originates statements.
tldr.outcome: It gives the IETF a consistent procedure for working with other organizations. The tools it describes are examples only, and it is a Best Current Practice (BCP 103).

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4053 describes how the IETF generates and handles liaison statements exchanged with other standards development organizations (SDOs), consortia and industry fora, so that the IETF can collaborate in the international standards community. The statements are mainly exchanged with organizations with which the IAB has set up a liaison relationship (see RFC 4052), though others are not precluded.

The procedures cover every liaison statement received from an SDO, whether or not a formal arrangement exists. Without a formal arrangement, the IETF is not obligated to respond.

The supporting tools are expected to arrive in at least three phases: a prototype, an operational tool without automated tracking, and a tool with tracking. The tools and functions described are one possible way to provide support and are examples only, not a normative part of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF gets letters from other groups. This document explains how to deal with them, but the exact computer tools it mentions are just examples.

sections.title: Definitions and Roles
sections.content:
A liaison statement is a business letter sent by one standards organization to another, usually between peers at any level such as a WG or an Area. Its purpose is generally to ask for information, make a comment or request an action. The expectations in this part are normative for statements sent by any SDO to the IETF.

The RFC defines four terms:

  • Addressee: the Working Group(s) or other party(s) in the IETF the statement is addressed to.
  • Assignee: the person responsible for acting on it, initially the addressed person or the chair of the addressed group. The task may be reassigned.
  • Liaison manager: a person who manages the relationship with a peer organization so that communication is maintained, productive and timely.
  • Liaison statement: a letter exchanged between organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter has a person it is for, a person who must deal with it, and a go-between who looks after the friendship between the two groups.

sections.title: What a Liaison Statement Contains
sections.content:
Every statement carries envelope fields: From, To, Title, Response Contact (an email address for the reply), Technical Contact (one or more addresses for clarification), Purpose and Deadline. The statement must state its purpose with one of the labels For Information, For Comment, For Action or In Response.

Statements asking for comment or action indicate when it is required. If the addressee cannot meet the deadline, courtesy calls for a reply offering a more doable deadline or an alternative.

The content part has a Body and optional Attachments, which may be documents or URLs, including Internet Drafts. Because IETF participants use many systems, enclosed documents should be PDF, W3C HTML without proprietary extensions, or ASCII text. A proprietary file such as Microsoft Word may be sent but should come with a generally readable one.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter says who it is from and to, what it is about, who to answer, what it wants, and by when. Attached papers should be in formats everyone can open.

sections.title: Addressee Duties and Lifetime
sections.content:
The addressee treats a liaison statement like any business letter: it deserves appropriate consideration and, if a reply is requested and a suitable relationship exists, a courteous authoritative reply within the expected time. The reply might say the information was useful or not, that the action is done or will be done by a date, that it will not be done and why, or give an answer.

If a statement seems misdirected, the assignee should promptly ask the liaison manager to redirect it. If several IETF groups are involved, one assignee takes the lead on the response. An informational statement with no deadline still calls for a courteous thank-you statement, so the sender knows it arrived.

A liaison statement is a temporary document, much like an Internet Draft. Yet it is often the only IETF record of communication with the peer SDO, so fully dealt-with statements are archived, along with relevant attachments, in a way obviously distinct from current ones.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter should get a polite answer on time, even if the answer is no. If it went to the wrong desk, say so quickly. Old letters get filed away where they will not be mixed with new ones.

sections.title: Handling Incoming Statements
sections.content:
The IETF offers three electronic facilities: a submission form, a way of organizing and showing the contents, and a tracking system. At first, tracking is a manual procedure run by the liaison manager, with automation expected later.

The IETF Secretariat provides the submission form, which asks for the information in the contents section above. A submission results in these actions:

  • A display is created with the envelope data and URLs for the content items, plus whether and when the statement was answered.
  • A URL is added to the summary of outstanding liaison statements.
  • Once tracking is automated, a status entry is made for the relevant chair or AD.
  • An email goes to the assignee, copying the technical contacts, the assignee's supervisor (the relevant ADs for a WG, or the IETF Chair for an AD), the liaison manager for the sending SDO, and an alias such as an open mailing list.

The assignee can reply, change dates, reassign or close the statement. The liaison manager or tracking system periodically sends a reminder email, copied to everyone above except the mailing alias.
sections.plainLanguage: A web form takes in the letter, posts it on a public board, and sends an email to the person who must deal with it. Reminders keep coming until the job is closed.

sections.title: Sending and Answering Statements
sections.content:
Statements to other organizations can come from a WG, Area or the IETF as a whole. The (co)chairs judge how much consensus exists and decide the content, and the amount of consensus needed varies with the content.

Easy cases are sending a Standards Track RFC (Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Internet Standard, BCP), any WG document expected to go on the standards track, or an informational document that reflects a WG position. The document status must be clearly noted, and a WG draft is only Work in Progress. Individual Internet Drafts, Experimental or Historical RFCs and non-WG informational documents should not be sent without further consensus.

Requests for information need little consensus building. Requests for comments on a standards track WG draft need some consensus on the open mailing list. Requests that another body change, start or stop a work item are serious and need the clearest possible consensus.

Incoming statements marked For Comment or For Action require a response by the deadline, and the addressed group's (co)chairs must ensure it. If a comment request produces no clear consensus, a summary of the comments, or of the lack of interest, is still sent, labelled "collected comments". For an action request the IETF need not comply, but it must always tell the originator what it decided, giving reasons if it declines or modifies. Long tasks may need several status statements, the first by the original deadline.
sections.plainLanguage: Before writing to another group, check that your own group agrees. When a letter asks for an opinion or a favour, you must answer on time, even if the answer is that opinions differ or that you cannot do it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main concern in designing the process was a possible denial of service attack on the IETF and its processes. The RFC notes that the IETF has historically not always handled statements effectively, frustrating people elsewhere, and that some organizations have used the process to impose deadlines on IETF activities, which the IETF does not accept.

For this reason submission is automated: the IETF cannot rate-limit submitters, but it can manage its internal pipelines. The problem is worsened by the lack of any authentication of submitters. The IAB considers it important to accept statements whether or not a liaison relationship exists, so authenticating submitters would not be an effective control.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can drop letters in the mailbox, someone could flood it. So the mailbox is automatic, and the club keeps its own sorting line from getting overloaded.

items.label: For Information
items.desc: Informs the addressee of something and expects no response.

items.label: For Comment
items.desc: Requests commentary, usually within a stated time frame.

items.label: For Action
items.desc: Requests that the addressee do something on the sender's behalf, usually within a stated time frame.

items.label: In Response
items.desc: Responds to a peer organization's statement and expects no further response.
